notes:
I've written notes on each verse of Luke 7:26–50 below, but they are uneven. The research tools ran out, so a few things are missing:

- **Catholic and Orthodox pages:** I didn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic material below comes second-hand, through bible.org and the Catholic Bible translations shown on biblehub.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage.
- **Verses 26–28 on Enduring Word:** the page cut off just before Guzik's comments on these verses.
- **NET Bible notes without citation markers:** I read the NET notes for vv. 36–50, but some came through without citation markers. Those points have only the URL: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50

---

**v. 26–27**
- Traditional reading: John stands out because of his task as forerunner, which fulfils Malachi 3:1. His greatness is tied to his prophetic office and his mission to prepare the way for Jesus, fulfilling prophecies such as Malachi 3:1. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/7-28.htm
- Constable says Jesus identified John as the forerunner of Messiah predicted in Malachi 3:1. As Messiah's forerunner, John enjoyed a role greater than any other prophet, even those who gave messianic prophecies. Coffman says Jesus identified John as the "Elijah" who was to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-28.html

**v. 28** (traditions differ here)
- Usual reading: the difference is one of era and privilege, not character. In the NET notes, After John comes a shift of eras. The new era is so great that the lowest member of it (the one who is least in the kingdom of God) is greater than the greatest one of the previous era. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Luk+7%3A27%2C28
- Reformed (R.C. Sproul): the least in the kingdom is in a greater state of blessedness than John. Although John appears in the New Testament, he still belonged to the period of redemptive history called the Old Testament. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/message-john-baptist-part-2
- Baptist (John MacArthur) says outright that the verse doesn't shut John out: The kingdom of God is the realm of salvation where God rules over His people, and John was in the kingdom. For him the difference is "privileged revelation", not personal character. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-99/the-greatest-man-who-ever-lived-part-3
- Other Protestant views, on the same StudyLight page (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-28.html):
  - Coffman (Church of Christ) takes the opposite view to MacArthur: John the Baptist was not in the kingdom of Christ, the same not being set up until after John's death, and "greater" means privilege, not character.
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel, dispensational) contrasts dispensations: the old one, where God related to man in a legal way, through the law, and the present one.
  - Matthew Henry applies the verse to the least gospel minister, who holds a more honourable office than John.
  - Barclay rejects the idea that John ranks lower because he wavered. Instead, it was because John marked a dividing line in history.
- Patristic minority view (Pulpit Commentary): By "the least" we prefer, then, with Chrysostom and other ancient Fathers, to understand Jesus himself, meaning Jesus was "lesser" in age and in public estimation. Ellicott mentions this view but prefers the usual reading. https://biblehub.com/luke/7-28.htm

**v. 29–30**
- Barnes: the tax collectors "showed" that they approved of the message of God by submitting to the ordinance which he commanded. He takes these verses as Jesus still speaking, not as Luke's comment: Among the common people he was approved and obeyed among the rich and learned he was despised. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/luke/7-35.html
- Modern scholarship (D.A. Carson, TGC): both v. 29 and v. 35 use the same Greek verb ("justify"). For that reason most scholars conclude that in Luke Wisdom's children are «all the people, even the tax collectors," over against the religious authorities who listened to neither the Baptist nor Jesus. https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/documents/carson/1994_Matt_11.19b_Luke_7.35.pdf

**v. 31–32**
- The picture of children in the market: The simile is taken from children imitating in games a marriage or a funeral, with the accompaniments of merry or mournful music (Preacher's Homiletical, quoting the Speaker's Commentary). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-32.html
- Chuck Smith reads it as "What do you want?": You are in a position that nothing satisfies you. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-35.html

**v. 33–34**
- F.W. Robertson: The wisdom of a Divine life had appeared in two forms — ascetic in John the Baptist, social in Christ. The world recognized it in neither. In John they said it was insanity; in Christ worldliness and irreligion. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/7-35.htm

**v. 35** (many readings)
- Calvin lists several interpretations, including an ironic one. He prefers this: Wisdom, however wickedly she may be slandered by her own sons, loses nothing of her worth or rank, but remains unimpaired.
- Methodist (Adam Clarke): "children of wisdom" is a Hebrew idiom for the fruits of wisdom. He notes that some manuscripts of Matthew 11:19 read "works" instead of "children". Both points: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-35.html
- Gill (Baptist): wisdom is Christ, who is the wisdom of God, and his "children" are the people he saved. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/leb/luke/7-35.html
- Matthew Henry reads it as God will be glorified in the salvation of a chosen remnant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-29.html
- Cambridge Bible: the children are those of that generation who accepted the baptism of John and the ministry of Jesus, without making a stumbling-block of their different methods. Bornemann's view is mentioned there too: the verse is the critics' own ironic words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/7-35.htm
- Constable: the story that follows illustrates v. 35. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html

**v. 36**
- Preceptaustin: LUKE alone records the anointing of our Lord in the house of a Pharisee. This man had perhaps invited Jesus out of curiosity or admiration. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary
- NET note: people ate reclining on their side, head toward a low table and feet away from it. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50

**v. 37** (who was she?)
- Guzik (Enduring Word): Some suppose this was Mary Magdalene, but we have no evidence of this. In John 12:3 Mary of Bethany also anointed Jesus' feet with oil, but this was a separate incident. He says most take her to have been a prostitute, and suggests Jesus may have forgiven her before this meal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/
- Gill also says she was not Mary Magdalene or Mary of Bethany. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/7-37.htm
- Leon Morris, quoted on bible.org: Some have held that Luke's 'sinner' was Mary Magdalene, but this is sheer speculation. https://bible.org/seriespage/wordless-worship-unnamed-woman-luke-736-50
- NET notes:
  - This is a different event from the anointing in Jesus' last week. That woman was not a sinner, and that host, Simon the leper, could never have been a Pharisee.
  - The jar's neck usually had to be broken to open it, and perfume like nard could cost up to a year's wages.
  - Teachers often ate at open meals where listeners were welcome, but for her to approach Jesus took great nerve.
  - All three points: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50

**v. 38**
- Background (IVP, quoted at Preceptaustin): she was behind him at his feet because guests reclined with their feet toward the wall. Because perfume may have been a tool of her trade, Jesus accepting it would offend religious people. Preceptaustin also points out that the Greek verbs show repeated action: she kept wiping, kept kissing, kept anointing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary
- Poole: the hair she once used to attract lovers she now useth to testify her abhorrence of her former courses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/7-37.htm
- Barnes: she testified her love for the Lord Jesus, and at the same time her humility and sense of sin by kissing his feet. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-38.html

**v. 39**
- NET note: the Greek is a "contrary to fact" condition, as if Simon were saying "if he were a prophet (but he isn't)". Pharisees practised a separatism that ruled out contact with such a woman, and as Simon denies Jesus is a prophet, Jesus reads his thoughts. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50
- Chuck Smith: touching her would make you unclean. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html
- Preceptaustin: a physician does not spurn thesick—they are the very people it is in His mission to receive and to help. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary

**v. 40–43**
- NET notes: a denarius was about a day's wage, so the debts were roughly two months' and twenty months' pay. The verb for "forgave" pictures God's grace, not earned but bestowed with faith. That quote is from a different NET note; the debt figures and the verb note are at https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50
- Matthew Henry: by the parable Jesus forces Simon to acknowledge that the greater sinner this woman had been the greater love she ought to show to Jesus Christ when her sins were pardoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html

**v. 44–46**
- Bible.org: All through the dinner, Jesus' back was to the woman. Preceptaustin adds that Jesus turns to face her only after the parable. https://bible.org/seriespage/23-wordless-worship-unnamed-woman-luke-736-50 and https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary
- NET note: scholars disagree whether a host was required to offer these courtesies. Most think not, which makes what she did even more striking. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50
- Preceptaustin: Everything the woman did to Jesus, Simon had neglected to do. There are sins of omission as well as sins of commission. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary

**v. 47** (the main dispute: is love the cause of forgiveness or the evidence of it?)
- Protestant consensus: her love is the evidence, not the cause. This is broadly shared across traditions:
  - Reformed (Calvin): loving is not here said to be the cause of pardon but a later sign, so that "the free pardon of sins comes first in order".
  - Matthew Henry: he did not forgive us because we first loved him.
  - Constable points to v. 50: faith, not love, saved her.
  - All three: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html
- Baptist:
  - Gill: forgiveness is the cause and love the effect. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/luke/7-47.html
  - Alexander Maclaren: the love does not go before the forgiveness, but the forgiveness goes before the love. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/love-and-forgiveness.cfm
- Methodist: Clarke reads it as "therefore she loved much". Reading it the other way would be causing the tree to produce the root. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/luke/7-47.html Wesley's 1755 New Testament translates it "therefore she loved much". https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/luke/7-47.html
- Lutheran: Meyer notes that Bengel and Calovius read it the same way. Calovius says Christ "proves a posteriori", that is, from the effect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/7-47.htm
- Disagreement on timing (when did she know she was forgiven?):
  - Spurgeon: It was proved that she was forgiven, for she loved much, but she had never received the full assurance of it. She was a hopeful penitent rather than a confirmed believer. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-woman-which-was-a-sinner/
  - William Kelly (Brethren): she came truly penitent, full of love to His person, but not yet with the knowledge of her sins forgiven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html
  - Guzik (Enduring Word, the source listed under Pentecostal/charismatic) says she was forgiven probably privately on a prior occasion and now publicly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/
- A both-ways reading: one commentator on the BibleHub page (not named in what I read) says Her love and her forgiveness were mingled with each other in mutual interchange. She loved because she was forgiven; she was forgiven because she loved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/7-47.htm
- Modern scholarship (NET note): the Greek word "for" (*hoti*) here gives the evidence of forgiveness, not the ground. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50
- Catholic, second-hand only: a commentator quoted on bible.org says the "love won forgiveness" reading is the interpretation of Roman Catholic commentators (see Schanz), and the doctrine of contritio caritate formata is built upon it. (That Latin phrase means contrition shaped by love.) https://bible.org/seriespage/wordless-worship-unnamed-woman-luke-736-50 Translations differ too:
  - The Douay-Rheims has Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much.
  - The modern Catholic New American Bible has her many sins have been forgiven; hence, she has shown great love.
  - Both: https://biblehub.com/catholic/luke/7-47.htm
  - I couldn't check a Catholic or Orthodox source directly.
- Second half of the verse (Ellicott): the point is not that Simon's sins were few, but that he thought them few. https://biblehub.com/luke/7-47.htm
- Pulpit Commentary heads off an abuse of the verse: someone might say men should "sin freely in order that they may love greatly". It answers with Paul's reply in Romans 6. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/7-47.htm

**v. 48**
- Spurgeon: from that moment full assurance of faith must have occupied her soul. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-woman-which-was-a-sinner/
- Kelly: until Jesus said it, it would have been presumption for anyone at that time to act as if certain of forgiveness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html

**v. 49**
- BibleHub Study Bible: in Jewish practice forgiveness was linked to temple sacrifice, but Jesus offers forgiveness directly, showcasing His divine authority. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/7-47.htm
- GotQuestions: Jesus was revealing to them that He Himself was God. https://www.gotquestions.org/Simon-the-Pharisee.html
- NET note: compare the earlier dispute over Jesus forgiving sins in Luke 5:17–26. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50

**v. 50**
- Utley (bible.org): "has saved" is a Greek perfect tense, and This woman's expression of love was the result, not the means, of forgiveness. Faith in Christ is the key issue. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21304
- Preceptaustin: her faith (Lk 7:50), not the act of anointing Jesus' feet, was the instrument by which she laid hold of His forgiveness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-7-commentary
- Matthew Henry: her tears and love were the effects and products of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/7-47.html
- NET note: the event is a concrete example of Luke 5:31-32. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=luk+7%3A36-50
- Guzik: Jesus didn't want her to stay low at his feet. He raised her up, acknowledged her love, forgave her sin, and sent her in peace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/
- Wesley's sermon "Saving Faith" uses this woman as an example: she loved much, for she had much forgiven. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/7-47.htm
